titleStmt.title: Applying the Peak Over Thresholds Method on Worst-Case Response Time Analysis of Complex Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: Applying the Peak Over Thresholds Method on Worst-Case Response Time Analysis of Complex Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The predictability of timing behavior is a very important performance issue of a real-time system. As the complexity of modern industrial systems increases, analyzing the timing behaviors of those systems becomes more and more challenging. Most of the existing analysis methods depend on static and detailed information of the systems under analysis. However, sometimes only partial information of a system can be available, or it may require too much effort on obtaining those details, making those analysis methods much less feasible. Moreover, those methods usually focus on some specific system models with unrealistic assumptions, consequently, applying those methods on a complex industrial real-time system may result in overly pessimistic results. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a statistical method to compute Worst-Case Response Times (WCRTs) of complex real-time systems regarding soft timing constraints, which can provide a higher general applicability with less required system information. Our approach employs a Peak Over Thresholds (POT) method, which is a branch of the Extreme Value Theory (EVT). For the evaluation, we have applied this approach on the analysis of message transmission latencies over Controller Area Networks (CAN).

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The complexity of a modern real-time system is growing dramatically. For example, in a modern vehicle control system, there can be up to 100 Electronic Control Units (ECU) with hundreds of tasks, and several communication buses with hundreds of messages. Different ECUs may employ different scheduling mechanisms (e.g. priority-based scheduling or First-Come-First-Serve (FCFS)), and communication buses may use different protocols (e.g. Controller Area Networks (CAN) or FlexRay). For those systems, predicting timing behaviors, which is an important performance issue of realtime systems, becomes more and more challenging. One primary reason, we believe, is that most of the traditional analysis methods rely on specific system models which cannot accurately capture the behaviors of real complex systems. As a result, it is very difficult to apply those methods on modern industrial complex real-time systems.

A number of works have been proposed regarding timing analysis 1 of real-time systems in the past decades. The tra-ditional timing analysis is dominated by deterministic Response Time Analysis (RTA) 2 [1]. The first exact response time analysis was proposed by Joseph et al. in [2], which targets preemptive real-time systems with fixed priorities. Burns et al. extended that analysis later in [3] to handle non-preemptive behavior, and Audsley et al. [4] presented an extended analysis to support release jitter. A lot of other analysis methods have also been proposed regarding different additional system factors. In [5], Maki-Turja et al. presented a method extended from the traditional RTA, which captures execution time dependencies between tasks. In [6] and [7], the authors proposed approximate RTA for tasks with offsets, which was later extended by Maki-Turja and Nolin in [8] by introducing an efficient implementation method. Tindell et al. first applied the static RTA on timing analysis of CAN transmissions, which was later revised by Davis et al. in [9]. In [10], Yomsi et al. presented a RTA method for CAN messages with offsets, and in [11], the authors proposed an approach taking mixed message models into account. Moreover, in [12], the authors introduced an analysis approach for CAN messages where some nodes employ First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queues while other nodes use priority queues. Even though a number of solutions have been proposed so far regarding different system factors, it is still challenging to apply those methods on a real complex real-time system. One important reason is that the system models assumed in those methods may not accurately capture the randomness or unpredictability of a real system. On another hand, in order to provide guaranteed results, those methods need to assume some approximations in the analysis, which may include too much pessimism in complex scenarios. Moreover, those approaches usually depend on detailed system information, such as number of tasks, task parameters, scheduling policies and so on. In other words, if only partial system information is available, those solutions may not be applicable.

For hard real-time systems, where the timing requirements must be strictly satisfied, guaranteed upper bounds of WCRTs are very important due to safety issues. However, many systems, known as soft real-time systems, may not require those hard restrictions. These systems can afford some timing constraint violations up to some level, either due to the nature of those systems or by employing some mechanisms similar to fault tolerant schemes. For these systems, applying those methods, which may generate overly pessimistic WCRTs, may not be meaningful at all. Moreover, some system functions may be affected by average response times rather than worst-case scenarios, such as Lane Keeping and Lane Departure Warning [13]. Therefore, some stochastic timing analysis methods were proposed, that can provide either an estimation of WCRT with a probability, or a probability distribution of response times along with a confidence level. In [14], Bernat et al. presented a method to compute probabilistic bounds on task execution times of the worst-case path of code sections. Gardner and Liu [15] introduced a stochastic time demand analysis method to compute a lower bound of task deadline meeting percentage assuming a fixed priority scheduling policy. In [16], the authors presented a probabilistic analysis method for periodic realtime systems, which can support both static and dynamic priority based scheduling policies with arbitrary deadlines. Some stochastic analysis methods have also been proposed for timing analysis of real-time communications. In [17], Nolte et al. presented an analysis approach for CAN considering probability distributions of stuff-bits. The method presented in [18] provides a probabilistic analysis of communication delays of CAN based real-time systems, which takes task response times as well as sampling delays into account. Most of these methods still require detailed system information, and may employ some unrealistic assumptions.

Statistics based methods are another type of solutions for timing analysis of real-time systems, which depend on samples collected from real systems or some approved simulators. These methods usually require much more relaxed assumptions on analyzed systems, and can be generally applied on different systems without knowledge of all detailed system information. Zeng et al. have presented a statistical method in [13] to compute probability distributions of message response times in CAN, using a mixed model of the Gamma distribution and the Degenerate distribution. In [19] and [20], the authors applied the Extreme Value Theory (EVT), which is usually used to handle extreme scenarios of some events, on the analysis of Worst-Case Execution Time (WCETs). Considering the nature of WCETs, the Gumbel Max distribution is selected as the fitted probability distribution, which is used to model the maximum extreme cases [21]. In [22], the authors extended these works to the analysis of WCRTs, along with a systematic analysis framework. These EVT based analysis methods can be generally applied on different systems, since the system under analysis is considered as a black box without detailed information.

There are two types of analysis methods involved in EVT: one of them is the block maxima method which is the essence of the approaches presented in [20] [22] and [23]; and the other one is the Peak Over Thresholds (POT) approach which, as far as we know, has not been applied on the timing analysis of real-time systems. In this paper, we present a framework for applying POT theory on timing analysis of complex realtime systems. Similar to other statistics based analysis, this framework completely relies on the collected samples which may not cover all the possible scenarios. As a result, our analysis is more suitable for systems with soft real-time constraints, since it provides probabilistic approximations of WCRTs rather than deterministic results. This analysis method is also system independent by employing a black box view of an analyzed system. The approach is evaluated using three different case studies of message communications over a CAN based system. Comparisons between our method and the block maxima based approach are also provided.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces some basic background knowledge of the statistical tools used in our approach. In Section III, we illustrate our analysis framework in more details. The results of three case studies along with some comparison and discussion are presented in Section IV. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section V.

div.head: II. EXTREME VALUE THEORY
div.p: Extreme value theory is a statistical tool widely utilized in many different disciplines, which is usually used to deal with extreme cases of an event. Instead of analyzing the whole probability distribution of a data set, EVT focuses more on the tails (i.e. extreme deviations from the median of a distribution). EVT has been applied on predicting the size of freak waves, mutational events during evolution, the amounts of large insurance losses, and so on. Similar to the above examples, in a real-time system, the worst-case scenario can also be considered as a rarely occurring event. Therefore, EVT can be an appropriate tool to analyze extreme timing behaviors (i.e. WCETs and WCRTs) of complex real-time systems.
Two approaches exist in EVT to fit the tail of the probability distribution of collected samples: block maxima (minima) and peak over thresholds.

div.head: A. Block Maxima
div.p: The basic idea of block maxima (minima) is to analyze the sub data set comprised of the maximum (minimum) sample of each data block, where each block contains the same number of samples from the original population. Block maxima refers to the upper tail of the analyzed parent probability distribution, which matches the concept of the worst-case timing behaviors. On the other hand, block minima targets to the lower tail of the parent distribution, which relates to the best-case timing behaviors. Therefore, in this paper, we only discuss the block maxima approach.

The basic procedure of the Block Maxima (BM) approach is illustrated in Figure 1. a. Assume that the original data set is X = {x 1 , x 2 ,...,x N }, which contains N independent random samples following the same probability distribution. b. Divide the data set X into s blocks, where each block X i contains the same number (i.e. n) of samples. The estimation process includes fitting an appropriate distribution, best-fit parameter selection, and estimated upper bound computation. As discussed in [24], as the number (i.e. n) of samples within each block goes to infinity, the probability distribution of the sub data set M will converge to the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution. According to different values of the shape parameter ξ, GEV is categorized into three types of distributions: Type I -Gumbel distribution, with an unbounded non-heavy upper tail; Type II -Fréchet distribution, with a heavy upper tail and a bounded lower tail; Type III -Weibull distribution, with a bounded upper tail. Due to specific natures of different applications, the bestfit distribution needs to be selected accordingly. In [20] and [22], the authors use the Gumbel (Max) distribution to analyze WCETs and WCRTs respectively.

div.head: B. Peak Over Threshold
div.p: The Peak Over Threshold (POT) method relies on a sub data set generated from an original data set, where the samples in this sub data set must exceed a certain threshold or fall below a selected threshold. Similar to the discussion in Section II-A, we only focus on the former definition which relates to the upper tail of the parent distribution. As the threshold μ goes to infinity, the distribution of exceedances Y asymptotes to a limit distribution called the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD). According to the Cumulative Density Function (CDF) of GPD,

For a parent data set, if the probability distribution of a sub data set generated by the BM method asymptotes to a GEV, then the distribution of exceedances provided by the POT approach will asymptote to a GPD. The shape parameters of the fitted GEV and GPD distributions are identical, and the scale parameters are related. The outline of proofs has been given in [24].

BM and POT have been utilized in many different disciplines. BM is easier to apply in practice due to the straightforward procedure. However, sometimes the estimation uncertainties can be large because of a small sample size. On the other hand, POT may not be as easy to practically apply as BM due to diagnostics for threshold selection. A too low threshold may incur bias in the result, and a too high threshold may result in insufficient remaining samples. Once an appropriate threshold is selected, POT can be more efficient and stable than BM. Therefore, while choosing a suitable analysis approach, a system analyzer can balance the pros and cons of each method according to the analyzed data.

div.head: III. POT-BASED WORST-CASE RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
A. System Model
div.p: In our POT-based method, the system under analysis is considered as a black box, which means that we do not presume any assumptions regarding system properties such as scheduling policies and system architecture. Moreover, there is no assumption on tasks within a system either. In other words, task parameters can be selected arbitrarily, and partial task information can even be unknown.

div.head: B. WCRT Analysis 1) Sampling:
div.p: Statistics based methods totally rely on the samples used in the analysis. In order to achieve an accurate analysis, the quality and quantity of analyzed samples are both very important.

For the WCRT analysis, the data can be collected from either a real system or a simulator. The utilized simulator should be verified such that it can imitate the behaviors of the target system correctly. Obviously, the former choice may be more accurate, since no simulator can model a system better than the system itself. However, collecting samples from a real system may require more efforts on data extraction. For example, some assistant time-tracing programs are required to obtain the response times of a task in a real system, while this functionality can be more easily inserted in a well designed simulator. On another hand, if we want to modify some system properties, it may be easier to change the configurations on a simulator rather than a real system. Moreover, sometimes a fully completed real system may not be available, especially in the design phase. Therefore, different options can be selected according to specific scenarios.

One important requirement for EVT is that the analyzed samples should be Independent and Identically Distributed (IID). If the occurrence of one sample does not affect the result of another sample, then we can consider these two samples to be independent [24]. We can consider the original data population as a two-dimensional matrix. One dimension refers to variations between different system runs, such as variable initial phases. The other dimension relates to concrete task properties within each system run. In other words, if we collect m samples within each system run, and create the analyzed data set from n system runs in total, then the collected data can form an m × n matrix. However, due to the IID requirement, we cannot accept all the samples collected from the same system run. The reason is that an instance of a task may experience interference from another instance of the same task, as a result, the response times of these two instances are not independent. It can be easily observed from a periodic task when the response time of an instance can be larger than the period. For many complicated statistical applications in reality, it may be very difficult to guarantee the independencies of the collected samples. Therefore, instead of collecting completely independent samples, many applications employ some declustering mechanisms [24] to maximumly reduce the dependencies between the analyzed samples.

Another possible solution for our case is to use the concept of busy period (Figure 3), which represents the time interval starting from the end of a system idle interval until the start of the next idle interval. In other words, a busy period is a continuous time interval when the shared resource is occupied by at least one task. Assuming all the tasks do not suspend themselves, if we remove a job of a task τ i in a certain busy period, the length of this busy period will never increase. In other words, the idle time between this busy period and the successive busy period will not decrease. As long as the idle time does not decrease to 0, the jobs within different busy periods will not interference each other. As a result, the response time of another instance from the same task τ i in another busy period would not be affected. Therefore, the dependencies between samples can be dramatically decreased by picking only one sample from each busy period. However, for a complex system with multiple shared resources (e.g. processors and communication buses in a distributed real-time system) or self-suspended tasks, this approach may not be sufficient. Moreover, the corresponding implementation may also be quite challenging for complex systems. Therefore, in this paper, we use a more general solution that is picking only the maximum sample of each isolated system run3 (Algorithm 1, line 1 to line 6). In this case, we can acquire an one-dimensional data set, where all the samples are independent. Moreover, these samples are from the same distribution, which represents the response times of the corresponding task. Therefore, the formed data set is able to satisfy IID. This solution is easy to implement, however, we need to confess that the processing overhead will be increased as a price.
Besides the quality of the analyzed data set, the sample size is also very important. More collected samples can

Many statisticians have contributed to determining proper sample sizes of a statistical analysis. In this paper, the selection of sample size is based on the laws discussed in [25]. Several accuracy factors need to be taken into account while deciding an appropriate sample size, including: 1) margin of error, which relates to the expected precision level of results; 2) Confidence Level (CL), which denotes the representative level of the samples regarding the whole population; 3) degree of variability, which represents the variability level of the samples; 4) estimated population size. Determining those accuracy factors depend on the nature of an analyzed application and the target of the analysis. More details can be found in [25] and [26]. The case studies used in this paper are based on some suggested sample sizes from the above references.

As presented above, in our analysis, we convert a twodimensional matrix into a one-dimensional data set. The sample size determination needs to be considered separately on each dimension. 2) Threshold Selection: The primary idea of POT methods is to analyze the samples that exceed a certain threshold. The threshold needs to be selected carefully in order to guarantee the quality of the analysis results. A higher threshold may generate a better GPD approximation, but may incur too few acceptable samples after the sample filtering process. On the contrary, a lower threshold may produce a more reliable estimation with more available samples, but may include bias in results. There is no strict definition of an exactly correct threshold. Therefore, for different applications, we need to balance the trade-offs while choosing relatively appropriate thresholds.

A number of threshold selection methods have been proposed so far. In [27], the authors introduced several means to define a reasonable threshold, including the shape parameter based approach, the mean of excesses based method, the Lmoments based solution and so on. More related information can also be found in [28]. In this paper, our threshold selection process is based on the theory proved in [24].

For a sufficient large threshold, the estimated GPD is supposed to be independent of the threshold. In other words, if μ is a large enough threshold, the shape parameter ξ and the modified scale parameter (σ -ξ • μ) should be stable as μ increases. Theoretically, this is the definition of appropriate thresholds. However, in practice, the collected samples cannot form a smoothly continuous distribution, unless the sample size is extremely huge. For example, as shown in Figure 4, the probability distribution has a generally decreasing trend after the quantile of 7000. However, as the quantile increases gradually, the corresponding probability varies unstably (i.e. alternately increases and decreases). As a result, even though a threshold is large enough, it is still difficult to observe an infinite stability due to the limitation and uncertainty of collected samples.

As mentioned in Section II, if the probability distribution of a sub sample set, which is produced by applying BM on the parent data set, asymptotes to the GEV distribution, then the distribution of exceedances for a large threshold asymptotes to GPD. The estimated GEV distribution and GPD have identical shape parameters (see proofs in [24]). According to this theory, the shape parameter of GPD can be estimated based on the shape parameter of the corresponding GEV distribution. This is the basic theory of the threshold selection method used in our analysis.
The threshold selection process used in our analysis is achieved as follows: a)

Step 1: First, we apply the BM process on the collected data (Algorithm 1, line 7 to line 23). The number of samples in each data block increases iteratively until the sub data set can fit the GEV distribution. If the remaining number of blocks is smaller than the lowest bound N lb , the algorithm needs to be terminated due to insufficient samples used for estimation. In this paper, we employ the Chi Square Test as the Goodness of Fit (GoF) hypothesis test 4 , which is usually used to verify whether the selected samples come from a population with a specific distribution. The significance level p GoF of a GoF test is typically set to 0.05. Once the sub data set created from the BM process can pass the GoF test with the specific significance level, the best fit shape parameter ξ will be recorded for later steps. b) Step 2: Based on the shape parameter of the GEV distribution selected above, we can estimate an appropriate threshold (Algorithm 1, line 24 to line 40).

First, we need to create a set of threshold candidates (i.e. T hC), from where we will pick the final selected threshold. We divide the distance between the maximum sample and the minimum sample into a number (i.e. N thc ) of segments (i.e. granularity), the division points are selected as the threshold candidates.

Then, for each threshold candidate, samples from the parent data set DS M , which do not exceed this threshold candidate, will be filtered out. A sub data set is formed by the exceedance of the remaining samples (line 29 to line 33). If the sub sample set can fit the GPD with the given significance level p GoF , the best fit shape parameter will be recorded (line 34 to line 37). Finally, a suitable threshold can be selected based on the plot of shape parameters regarding different threshold candidates together with the shape parameter of the corresponding GEV distribution recorded in Step 1. We select a threshold based on two conditions: the shape parameter of the best fit GPD parameter should be close to the recorded GEV shape parameter; for the threshold candidates which are larger than the selected threshold, the shape parameters should keep relatively stable. Note that as we mentioned above, it is difficult to observe an infinity stability due to the uncertainty of collected samples, therefore, we only focus on obvious stable ranges. Finally, from the relatively convergence points (i.e. the marked dots along the distribution curves in Figure 5), we pick the one, whose shape parameter is the closest to the recorded GEV shape parameter, as the final selected threshold (i.e. the intersection points of the vertical dashed lines and the distribution curves in Figure 5). Note that close to the upper most tail (i.e. the left side of Figure 5), the shape parameters may vary a lot due to insufficient remaining samples. Therefore, these points are ignored in this process. The selected thresholds can also be verified based on modified scale parameters. As shown in Figure 6, when the threshold increases from the selected threshold, the modified scale parameter keeps relatively stable. 3) WCRT estimation: A sub data set DS F can be created from the parent sample set DS M , which contains the exceedances of samples greater than or equal to the selected threshold th F (Algorithm 1, line 41 to line 45). If the sub data set DS F can fit the GPD with the specific significance level p GoF , then we can compute an estimated WCRT using Eq. 2 (Algorithm 1, line 50 to line 52). Otherwise, a resampling method (e.g. bootstrapping [29]) is required.

The targeted exceedance probability p t is used for the percent point function of GPD. Due to the sample filtering process, the actual exceedance probability of the parent data set will be lower than p t . For a random sample in the parent data set DS M , the exceedance probability regarding the estimated WCRT can be approximately computed as

div.head: C. Applicability Discussion
div.p: As we discussed above, the analyzed system in this POT based approach is considered as a black box. The analysis only relies on the collected samples rather than the detailed system information. Therefore, this method can be generally applied on many different types of applications, even if only partial system information is available. However, similar to most other statistics based analysis methods, the overhead5 caused by the sample collection process may obviously limit the applicability of this approach. Similar to the discussions in [23], we would like to consider this POT based analysis as a complement of the classic RTA. This approach can be utilized in some complicated scenarios where the traditional RTA may not be feasible. For example, in the evaluation and validation phase of a system development process, the complexity of the analyzed system may be increased dramatically due to the integration of variant components and some unknown factors. As a result, it may be very difficult to predict all the information required by the traditional RTA. In this case, our POT based approach can be much more helpful since it is system independent.

Moreover, we need to emphasize that this POT based WCRT analysis is more suitable for soft real-time system, since it provides approximated (probabilistic) but not deterministic upper bounds of WCRTs. As we discussed above, statistics based analysis completely rely on the collected samples. A larger amount of analyzed data can usually produce more precise results. In order to provide extremely accurate results, we have to analyze a huge amount of samples, which may be infeasible in reality. Therefore, while utilizing statistics based analysis, system designers need to balance the tradeoff between the expected accuracy and the involved overhead based on the requirements of different applications.

div.head: IV. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we present three case studies to show the evaluation results of our analysis method. We apply our POT based approach on the worst-case transmission delay analysis of messages over a CAN bus. The case studies use the same network topology, which contains four ECUs connected with a CAN bus. The randomness considered in these case studies include processing delays, release jitters, stuff-bits percentage, and physical interference. We need to emphasize that the POT based analysis is system independent. In other words, our approach does not depend on any of the above system features.

While comparing the results from our method with the results generated by the BM based method [23], we set the exceedance probabilities for the parent data set (i.e. Pr(x > est), not p t ) of the two approaches to be identical. The targeted exceedance probability p t in our method is set to be 10 -5 , and the corresponding exceedance probability of BM based method is changed accordingly.

In [23], the comparisons between the BM based approach and the traditional RTA have already been presented. The results show that for the systems with lower complexities, the traditional RTA slightly outperforms the BM based analysis regarding the tightness of the results. While considering the generated results together with the processing overhead, the traditional RTA performs obviously better. However, when the complexity of an analyzed system increases, the traditional RTA no longer dominates. Sometime, the traditional RTA may incur 4 times more pessimism than the BM based analysis. Moreover, if partial information of those systems are unknown, the classic RTA cannot even be applied. Nevertheless, the statistics based analysis always works as long as enough samples, which can be collected from either a real system or an approved simulator, are provided. In the following experiments, we focus more on the comparisons between our POT based analysis and the BM based approach.

div.head: A. Case study 1
div.p: In this case study, the analyzed system is configured with a relatively lower complexity. There are five periodic message flows transmitted in the network, with a total utilization of 86.28%. All the ECUs use priority based queues. The message parameters and the results are presented in Table II. As shown in Figure 7, with the same exceedance probability, the results of our POT based approach are slightly tighter than the results using the BM based method. Results from both methods are very close to the results from long time simulations (i.e. less than 3.5% deviation). In the following result tables, these deviations are called 'pessimism', which is computed as WCRT (EST ) -WCRT (BP)

div.head: B. Case study 2
div.p: In this case study, the network is shared by 20 message flows generated from different ECUs, and all the ECUs still employ priority based queues. The total utilization is around 66.32%. The message parameters are listed in Table III. Five of these flows (F 9 , F 10 , F 12 , F 14 , and F 17 ) are configured to be sporadic, the corresponding periods listed in the table denote their minimum inter-arrival times.

We select five flows (F 1 , F 2 , F 3 , F 4 , F 5 ) as the analyzed flows. Comparing to Case Study 1, the complexity of this case study increases due to the larger number of flows and mixed flow models. As shown in Figure 8, in this case, the pessimism of the BM based approach goes up to 14%, while our method performs much more stable (i.e. less than 2% pessimism). Fig. 8. Comparison of the pessimism between our method and the BM based approach for 20 mixed flows.

div.head: C. Case study 3
div.p: As discussed in [12], in some systems, different ECUs may employ different message queues (i.e. FIFO queues or priority based queues). Therefore, in this case study, we configure the ECUs with different types of message queues. The CAN bus is shared by 50 mixed message flows with the total utilization around 70.15%. The message information is presented in Table IV.

First, all the ECUs (E 1 , E 2 , E 3 and E 4 ) are configured to use FIFO queues. Figure 9 shows the results of five analyzed flows. In this case study, given the same exceedance probability, our POT based approach can still generate tighter results than the BM based method. Then we change E 1 and E 3 to use priority based queues, while E 2 and E 4 still use FIFO queues. The comparison of results is displayed in Figure 10. Similar to the observations of the above comparisons, in this case, the estimated WCRTs using our method are still closer to the long time simulation results.

div.head: D. Discussions
div.p: In our test cases, the best practice simulation result of each flow is based on over one million samples. The results show that none of these samples exceeds the estimated WCRT generated by our POT based analysis. According to the above comparisons, it can be obviously noticed that given the same exceedance probability of a random sample from the parent data set, our POT based method can usually provide tighter results than the BM based approach. One reason is that the amount of the collected samples may be relatively small in our experiments (i.e. N BM ≤ 700 results in that sometimes the number of blocks becomes almost N lb ). As we mentioned before, when the sample size is low, the estimation uncertainties for the BM based approach can be very large.

However, we need to confess that the POT based method may include more overhead than the BM based approach, due to the threshold selection process. Therefore, the tradeoff between accuracy and overhead of an analysis needs to be balanced while choosing an appropriate method for different applications.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS
div.p: In this paper, we present a framework of applying the Peak Over Thresholds (POT) method on the analysis of worstcase response times, targeting soft complex real-time systems. Block Maxima (BM) and POT are the two approaches involved in the extreme value theory. The former method has been utilized in some related works ( [20] and [22]). However, to the best of our knowledge, the POT based analysis method has not been presented in the discipline of real-time systems so far. In order to evaluate our POT based approach, we use case studies of communication delay analysis for messages transmitted in a CAN bus based system. According to the evaluation results, given the same exceedance probability, our POT based method can usually provide tighter upper bounds on worst-case response times comparing to the BM based approach.

The POT based analysis is independent of system models, and can work well even when only partial system informa-tion is available. Due to these benefits, this method can be utilized for many applications, where most of the existing static response time analysis methods may not be feasible. However, similar to other statistics based analysis method, this approach may include more overhead because of the sampling process. Therefore, in the future we may try to optimize our solution by reducing the required sample size while keeping an acceptable accuracy. On another hand, we may also think about how to utilize the collected data to achieve other types of analysis rather than the worst-case timing analysis. The overhead may be somehow decreased by multiple employments of the collected samples. Moreover, we will further investigate this POT based approach by combining with other threshold selection methods.
